analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give pregnant workers reasonable accommodations, like light duty or schedule changes, unless it is an undue hardship.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill never got a floor vote: introduced June 16, 2022, placed on the Senate calendar the same week, and never scheduled for a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required employers with 15 or more workers to make reasonable accommodations for employees whose ability to do their job is limited by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions — for example, letting a worker keep working with modified duties instead of forcing her onto leave — unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the business. It allowed pregnant workers to sue under the same procedures and remedies as other employment discrimination claims, and it barred states from using constitutional immunity to escape those suits. The bill had bipartisan support from the start: Senator Bob Casey (D-PA) introduced it with Senator Bill Cassidy (R-LA), and Senator Patty Murray (D-WA) and Senator Richard Burr (R-NC) signed on. It was placed on the Senate calendar within a week of introduction, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers and applicants at employers with 15 or more employees. Under current law, many workers are pushed onto unpaid leave or out of their jobs for needing modest changes like lighter lifting or more bathroom breaks; this bill would have let them ask for an accommodation and sue if the employer refused, with the same remedies available in other discrimination cases. States could not shield themselves from such suits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pregnant workers needing modest job adjustments

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees would have to make reasonable accommodations to a worker's known limitations from pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions unless doing so would impose an undue hardship on the business.

Employers could not force a pregnant worker onto paid or unpaid leave if a reasonable accommodation would let her keep working, and could not deny job opportunities or take adverse action because a worker needed or used an accommodation.

The bill gives pregnant workers the same enforcement powers, remedies, and damages that apply under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and prohibits retaliation against anyone who asserts these rights.
The EEOC would have to issue regulations, within a year, spelling out examples of reasonable accommodations that must be provided absent an undue hardship.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would bear the cost of accommodations — though only ones that would not cause an undue hardship, and with a good-faith defense limiting money damages when an employer tried but failed to find a workable accommodation. The bill did not require employer health plans to cover any particular treatment.

drawbacks.text: Employers with 15 or more employees would bear new compliance and accommodation costs, and the bill gave them an undue-hardship escape only after a case-by-case fight, which can push disputes into litigation rather than resolve them.

The bill limits remedies: if an employer shows it made good-faith efforts, in consultation with the worker, to find an accommodation, no money damages are available for the accommodation claim itself [S3].

The bill strips states of their Eleventh Amendment immunity, letting state employees sue their own governments for violations — a federalism objection states and some senators have raised against similar provisions.
The 15-employee threshold leaves workers at smaller businesses, a large share of the private workforce, with no new protection under this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost to employers was limited by design: businesses with fewer than 15 employees were not covered, and the bill exempted accommodations that would impose an undue hardship, with a good-faith defense shielding employers from money damages when they had tried in consultation with the worker to find a workable accommodation [S2][S3]. Against that, workers would have gained a clear, enforceable right to keep working through pregnancy instead of being pushed onto unpaid leave or out of a job [S2]. The main weakness is that it relied on a complaint-and-litigation model — protection arrives only after a worker asserts a right — rather than guaranteeing anything up front.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill, put it on its calendar, and then simply never brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 16, 2022 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under 'Read the First Time'; on June 21 it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 425.
After June 21, 2022, the action history shows no further steps: no committee markup, no motion to proceed, no floor vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still on the calendar, and all bills not passed by then die and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more employees are better off, because they never had to provide the mandated accommodations or face related lawsuits. Pregnant workers gained nothing from this bill, though a separate House-passed version of the same proposal later became law in a different vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who avoided the accommodation mandate

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in the Senate on June 16, 2022.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan backing.

for.name: Sen. Richard Burr
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Carolina, then-ranking member of the HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was one of 2 of 50 Senate Republicans to do so.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington, Chair of the HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; she was one of 2 of 48 Senate Democrats listed as a cosponsor.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote; the action record shows nothing after it was placed on the Senate calendar in June 2022, and the Congress ended without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — its original cosponsors included two Republicans and two Democrats out of each party's caucus — but bipartisan sponsorship never translated into floor time, since the Senate's leaders never scheduled a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to provide reasonable accommodations to workers limited by pregnancy or childbirth, at their own expense, unless they could show an undue hardship. For the bill, avoiding that mandate meant keeping the existing system where pregnant workers can be pushed onto leave or out of jobs with no recourse.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and low-wage service employers
industries.note: Physically demanding, hourly workplaces — retail, warehouses, food service, health care — are where pregnant workers most often need accommodations like light duty or extra breaks, so the accommodation duty would have fallen heaviest there. Defeat of the bill left those workers with no federal right to such accommodations.
